title: Injection: when data becomes code
summary: SQL, NoSQL, OS command, template, LDAP, header and log injection from first principles: how parsers mix code and data, the fixed code next to the bug, and the cases that show what is at stake.
outcomes: Explain why concatenating untrusted data into code lets the data change the parsed structure
Read basic SQL and trace exactly how an input such as ' OR '1'='1 rewrites a query
Fix SQL injection with parameterised queries and allowlists, and explain why escaping is fragile
Spot injection in ORM raw queries, stored procedures, MongoDB filters, shell calls and templates
Apply least privilege so a successful injection reaches as little as possible
Use the Heartland, TalkTalk, MOVEit and Shellshock cases to reason about impact and response
Choose between validation, output encoding and parameterisation for each interpreter
Name the log signals that reveal injection probing and exploitation

lessons.title: When data becomes code: the one idea behind every injection

blocks.md:
Many programs build a piece of text in *another* language and hand it to an **interpreter**: a program that reads text and carries out what it says. A database reads SQL, a shell reads command lines, a template engine reads templates. Before an interpreter can act, it **parses** the text: it splits it into **tokens** (words, symbols, quoted strings, numbers) and decides which tokens are instructions (**code**) and which are values (**data**).

**Injection** is what happens when data from someone else ends up in that text and contains characters the parser treats as code. The outsider's input is *injected* (pushed into) the instructions and changes what they mean.

The smallest possible example uses Python's own interpreter. `eval()` takes a string and runs it as a Python expression. A shop wants the total for a quantity typed by the customer, and the programmer glues the input onto a formula with an f-string (a string prefixed with `f`, in which `{qty}` is replaced by the variable's value):

blocks.code:
price = 19
qty = request_param("qty")          # meant to be a number such as "3"

# VULNERABLE: builds code out of data, then runs it
total = eval(f"{price} * {qty}")

# qty = "3"           gives 57
# qty = "3 + 1000"    gives 1057  (the input added an operator)

# FIXED: turn the input into a value first; never build code from it
total = price * int(qty)            # "3 + 1000" now raises ValueError
blocks.caption: Run in Python 3. The fixed line can only ever multiply two numbers: int() either produces one integer or fails.

blocks.title: How the interpreter tokenises the built string

scenes.caption: Input "3". The string is `19 * 3`. The parser finds a number, an operator and a number: the structure the programmer intended. Only the last token came from the user.
Input "3 + 1000". The string is now `19 * 3 + 1000`. The user's text contained an operator, and the parser has no way to know which tokens were meant to be data.
Fixed: int("3") is a value, not text. Python multiplies 19 by 3 without parsing anything the user typed. Input "3 + 1000" is rejected by int() before any code runs.

blocks.md:
Every bug in this course has the same shape:

1. The program **concatenates** (joins end to end) trusted code and untrusted data into one string.
2. An interpreter **parses** that string.
3. Some characters in the data are special to that interpreter (a quote, a semicolon, a brace, a newline), so the data changes the structure.

CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration, a public catalogue of software weakness types run by MITRE, a US non-profit) files the whole family under [CWE-74](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/74.html), "Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Output Used by a Downstream Component". *Neutralization* means making special characters lose their special meaning. *Downstream component* is the interpreter that receives the string. The OWASP Top 10 (a ranking of the most critical web application risks, from the Open Worldwide Application Security Project) lists Injection as A05 in its 2025 edition; that category also includes cross-site scripting, which the client-side attacks course covers.

The idea is old. In December 1998 the hacker magazine *Phrack* (issue 54) carried an article by a researcher writing as rain.forest.puppy about Microsoft web servers talking to Microsoft SQL Server. It showed that a web page which pasted a form field into a database query let a visitor "piggyback SQL commands" onto it. The example page even connected to the database as `sa`, the all-powerful system administrator account. Lesson 8 returns to why that matters.

The interpreters you will meet: SQL databases (lessons 2 to 9), MongoDB-style NoSQL databases (10), the operating system shell (11 and 12), template engines (13), LDAP directories, XPath, HTTP headers and log files (14).

The fix for every injection is the same idea: keep code and data in **separate channels**, so the interpreter never has to guess which is which. For SQL that is a parameterised query, for the shell an argument list, for templates a template variable. Escaping and filtering are fallbacks for when no separate channel exists.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the shop instead stripped spaces from qty before the eval, so "3 + 1000" becomes "3+1000". Is the bug fixed?
blocks.reveal: No. `19 * 3+1000` still parses as an expression with an extra operator, because Python does not need spaces between tokens. Removing characters you thought were dangerous only removes the examples you thought of. The real fix changes the design: convert the input to a number, so there is no code string left to inject into.

blocks.question: Which statement best describes the root cause of an injection bug?
options: The attacker's input was too long for the buffer
Untrusted data was placed into a string that an interpreter later parsed as code
The server did not use HTTPS
The program trusted a cookie set by another origin
blocks.explain: Injection is a confusion between code and data inside one string. Length limits, HTTPS and cookie rules are other topics. The interpreter parses the combined string and cannot tell which part came from the user.

blocks.question: A program reads a city name and runs `eval("lookup('" + city + "')")`. A user types `Paris`. Another types `x') or delete_all('`. What does the second input do?
options: Nothing, because the city name is inside quotes
Python raises an error because quotes are not allowed in strings
It closes the quoted string early and adds a second function call to the expression
It only looks up a city literally named with those characters
blocks.explain: The built string becomes lookup('x') or delete_all(''). (Python's or runs delete_all only if lookup('x') returns a false value; an attacker would pick an operator that always runs the second call, but either way it is code the programmer never wrote.) The first quote in the input closes the string literal the programmer opened, so the rest is parsed as code. Quotes only protect data if the data cannot contain the closing quote.

lessons.title: SQL from zero: tables, queries, quotes and comments

blocks.md:
A **database** stores data so many programs can read and change it safely. A **relational** database keeps data in **tables**: each **row** is one record (one user) and each **column** is one property (username, role). The name comes from the relational model of Edgar F. Codd, an IBM researcher, in which a table is called a *relation*.

Programs talk to it in **SQL** (Structured Query Language). It was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald D. Chamberlin and Raymond F. Boyce under the name SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language), and was renamed SQL because SEQUEL was a trademark of another company (Chamberlin, *Early History of SQL*, 2012). PostgreSQL, used later in this course, descends from POSTGRES, a University of California, Berkeley research database, and was renamed to show it supports SQL. The program that runs the database is a DBMS (database management system): SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and Microsoft SQL Server are examples.

blocks.caption: A toy table used for the whole course, run with sqlite3. Real systems never store plain passwords; they store salted password hashes (the authentication course covers this). Plain text keeps the examples readable.

blocks.title: A WHERE clause picks rows

scenes.caption: Three rows, one per user, and four columns. (The password cell shows hunter2 shortened.)
SELECT * FROM users: no WHERE clause, so every row is returned.
SELECT username, role FROM users WHERE role = 'user': the condition is checked for each row; bob and cy match, and only two columns are returned.
WHERE username = 'ana' AND password = 'rose': both comparisons must be true. Only row 1 matches. This is the shape of a typical login query.

blocks.md:
The parts of a query, and the tokens the parser cares about:

- **Keywords** such as `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `AND`, `OR` are code.
- **Identifiers** name tables and columns: `users`, `role`.
- **Literals** are values written in the query. A **string literal** sits between single quotes, `'user'`. A number has no quotes, `2`.
- A single quote *inside* a string literal is written twice: `'it''s'` is the five-character text it's. This doubling is SQL's **escape** for the quote.
- `--` starts a **comment**: the parser ignores everything after it to the end of the line.
- `;` ends a statement, so one string can hold several statements.

blocks.code:
SELECT 'it''s';                                    -- it's
SELECT username FROM users;  -- everything after the two dashes is ignored
SELECT 1 OR 1 AND 0, (1 OR 1) AND 0;              -- 1|0   AND binds tighter than OR
SELECT name FROM products WHERE released = 1
UNION SELECT username FROM users;                 -- rows from both tables in one result

-- Changing data:
UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE id = 2;
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 3;
DROP TABLE users;                                 -- deletes the whole table
blocks.caption: Outputs from sqlite3 3.51. 1 means true and 0 false. UNION needs both SELECTs to return the same number of columns.

blocks.md:
Two rules matter later. First, **AND binds tighter than OR**, the way multiplication binds tighter than addition: `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`. Second, **UNION** glues the rows of a second SELECT onto the first, so one query can return data from two tables.

Whether one call may run several statements separated by `;` ("stacked queries") depends on the driver, the library a program uses to talk to the database. Python's `sqlite3` refuses: `execute()` raises "You can only execute one statement at a time". Microsoft SQL Server's batches accepted them, which is what the 1998 Phrack article relied on.

blocks.title: How the database evaluates a SELECT
blocks.code:
SELECT username
FROM users
WHERE id > 1
  AND role = 'user'
ORDER BY username;

scenes.caption: FROM is logically first: start with every row of the users table.
WHERE id > 1 drops ana (id 1). The literal 1 is a number, so it has no quotes.
AND role = 'user': both remaining rows match. 'user' is a string literal: the parser knows where it ends by finding the closing quote.
SELECT keeps only the username column.
ORDER BY sorts the result. Note where code (keywords, identifiers) and data (the literals 1 and 'user') sit: injection is about moving that boundary.

blocks.md: The SQL characters to remember for this course: `'` ends a string literal, `--` turns the rest of the line into a comment, `;` ends a statement, and the keywords `OR`, `AND` and `UNION` change which rows come back.

blocks.question: What does `SELECT 'O''Brien';` return?
options: A syntax error, because there are three quotes
The text O'Brien
The text O''Brien with two quotes
The text O, then a second statement Brien
blocks.explain: Inside a string literal, two single quotes in a row stand for one quote character. The literal is 'O''Brien' and its value is O'Brien. A lone quote in the same place would end the literal instead.

blocks.question: How does SQL read `WHERE username = 'ana' AND password = 'x' OR role = 'user'`?
options: username = 'ana' AND (password = 'x' OR role = 'user')
Left to right with no precedence
(username = 'ana' AND password = 'x') OR role = 'user'
It is a syntax error without parentheses
blocks.explain: AND binds tighter than OR, so the two AND-ed comparisons form one group and OR joins that group with role = 'user'. Every row with role user matches, whatever its username and password. Remember this for the next lesson.

lessons.title: SQL injection step by step: watching the query change

blocks.md: **SQL injection** (SQLi) is injection where the interpreter is a SQL database. Here is the login code that causes it. It uses a Python f-string (lesson 1). The result is ordinary text, built before the database sees anything.

blocks.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")

def login(username, password):
    # VULNERABLE: user input is pasted into the SQL text
    query = ("SELECT id, username FROM users "
             f"WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}'")
    rows = db.execute(query).fetchall()
    return rows[0] if rows else None    # log in as the first matching row
blocks.caption: The programmer put quotes around each value, expecting the value to stay inside them.

blocks.title: Four logins through the vulnerable function
blocks.code:
def login(username, password):
    query = ("SELECT id, username FROM users "
             f"WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}'")
    rows = db.execute(query).fetchall()
    return rows[0] if rows else None

scenes.caption: An honest login. Each value lands inside its quotes, and the query has the structure the programmer intended.
One row matches, so ana is logged in. A wrong password would return no rows and None.

scenes.output:
WHERE username = 'O'Brien' AND ...
error: near "Brien": syntax error
scenes.caption: A real surname with an apostrophe. The quote in the name closes the literal early, Brien is left over as garbage code, and the database refuses to parse it. The bug is visible before any attacker arrives.
The textbook illustration. The first quote closes the password literal, OR '1'='1' becomes new code, and the last quote is supplied by the programmer's own template.

AND binds tighter than OR, so the condition is (username = 'ana' AND password = '') OR '1'='1'. The right side is true for every row, all three rows return, and the code logs in as the first: ana, an admin.

blocks.title: The same query, token by token

scenes.caption: The end of the honest query: password = 'rose'. The whole literal 'rose' is one data token, as intended.
With the injected password, the parser now sees seven tokens. The user's characters produced an empty literal, a keyword and a comparison.

Mixed tokens are the key: '' starts with the programmer's quote and ends with the attacker's, and '1' at the end ends with the programmer's quote. The boundary between code and data is wherever the quotes say.

blocks.md:
Two more inputs that PortSwigger's Web Security Academy (the free training site run by PortSwigger, the company behind the Burp Suite testing proxy) uses as standard illustrations:

- Username `ana'--` with any password gives `WHERE username = 'ana'--' AND password = 'anything'`. Everything after `--` is a comment, so the password check disappears. Run against the toy table, it returns ana's row.
- A product filter that builds `WHERE category = 'Gifts' AND released = 1` can be cut short the same way, revealing unreleased products.

In each case the attacker does not need to guess a password; they rewrite the question the application asks.

blocks.code:
def login(username, password):
    # FIXED: the SQL text is a constant; values travel separately
    rows = db.execute(
        "SELECT id, username FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?",
        (username, password),
    ).fetchall()
    return rows[0] if rows else None

# login("ana", "' OR '1'='1")  gives None (no user has that password)
# login("O'Brien", "x")        gives None, no syntax error
# login("ana", "rose")         gives (1, 'ana')
blocks.caption: Each ? is a placeholder. The database receives the query text and the two values separately (lesson 7 shows exactly how). Outputs from sqlite3.

blocks.md: Removing the word OR, or blocking the quote character, is not a fix. It breaks real users (O'Brien, a shop in Portland OR) and misses inputs that need neither, such as a numeric field (lesson 6). The fix is to stop building SQL text out of input.

**Defender view.** The O'Brien error is also the attacker's first probe: PortSwigger lists submitting a single quote and watching for errors as the basic manual test. So the earliest signals are database syntax errors from a code path that never normally fails, and request parameters containing quotes, `--` or `OR`. Default web server access logs record only the URL line, so they show these in query strings (GET) but not in form bodies (POST, as in this login); seeing bodies needs a WAF or application logging. Lesson 15 shows the actual PostgreSQL log lines. Prevention is the fixed code above; response starts with finding every query built by concatenation, not just the one that was reported.

blocks.question: A login form is vulnerable as shown. An attacker types `ana'--` as the username and leaves the password blank. What happens?
options: The database reports a syntax error and nobody logs in
The query returns no rows, because the password is blank
The password check is commented out, so the query returns ana's row and the attacker is logged in as ana
Every user is logged in at once
blocks.explain: The query becomes WHERE username = 'ana'--' AND password = ''. The quote closes the username literal, and -- turns the rest, including the password check, into a comment. One row matches: ana.

blocks.question: Why does the honest username O'Brien break the vulnerable login?
options: The apostrophe closes the string literal early, leaving Brien to be parsed as SQL code
SQLite does not support apostrophes in TEXT columns
Python f-strings cannot contain quotes
The name is longer than the column allows
blocks.explain: The value is pasted between quotes, so its own quote ends the literal and the parser meets Brien where it expects a keyword. A parameterised query stores and matches O'Brien without trouble.

lessons.title: Beyond the login: UNION, blind and second-order injection

blocks.md: Once input can change the structure of a query, what an attacker can do depends on two things: **where** the input lands in the query (a WHERE value, an ORDER BY clause, an INSERT) and **what the application shows back** (the rows, an error, or nothing). PortSwigger groups the outcomes as retrieving hidden data, subverting application logic (the login bypass), UNION attacks and blind injection. This lesson stays at concept level: what each variant is, why it works, and what defenders see.

**UNION-based injection.** If the page displays the rows of a query, injected text can add `UNION SELECT ...` so that rows from a *different* table are glued onto the result. The database only accepts this when both SELECTs return the same number of columns with compatible types, so attackers first work out the column count. The product list then shows usernames or other data, because the page simply prints whatever rows come back.

blocks.title: What a product page prints after a UNION

scenes.caption: Normal page: the query selects released product names and the page lists them.

The injected UNION adds a second SELECT over the users table. The page code has not changed; it prints every row it receives, so usernames appear in the product list. (Simplified: real attacks first match the column count.)

blocks.md:
**Blind injection.** Often the page shows no query results and hides errors. The attacker can still ask yes or no questions, because something observable depends on whether an injected condition is true:

- **Boolean-based**: the page differs (say, a "Welcome back" message appears) when the condition is true.
- **Error-based**: a condition triggers a database error only when true, and the error changes the response.
- **Time-based**: a condition makes the query pause, so the response is slower when true.
- **Out-of-band**: the database is made to contact a server the attacker controls, for example through a DNS (Domain Name System) lookup.

Each request leaks about one bit, so tools automate thousands of requests. The best known is **sqlmap**, an open-source tool that detects and exploits SQL injection; use it only on your own lab. Defenders often spot it by its default User-Agent header, which starts with `sqlmap/`, and by the bursts of near-identical requests described below. Slow, but enough to read a whole table.

blocks.title: Blind injection leaks one bit per request (concept)

scenes.caption: The attacker sends a request whose injected condition asks a question, such as whether some value starts with a given letter.
The condition is true, the query finds a row, and the page shows its normal welcome message. No data is printed, but the attacker learned one fact.
Next question, condition B. False this time: no row, no welcome message. Repeating this thousands of times reconstructs data letter by letter.

blocks.md: **Second-order (stored) injection.** The input is stored safely, then used unsafely later by different code that trusts it because it came from the application's own database. A toy version, run in sqlite3:

blocks.code:
# Sign-up is safe: placeholders store the name exactly as typed.
db.execute("INSERT INTO users (username, password, role) VALUES (?, ?, 'user')",
           ("ana'--", "x"))

def change_password(current_user, new):
    # VULNERABLE: current_user came from our own database, "so it is safe"
    db.execute(f"UPDATE users SET password = '{new}' "
               f"WHERE username = '{current_user}'")

change_password("ana'--", "pwned")
# UPDATE users SET password = 'pwned' WHERE username = 'ana'--'
# The real admin ana now has password 'pwned'.

# FIXED
def change_password(current_user, new):
    db.execute("UPDATE users SET password = ? WHERE username = ?", (new, current_user))
blocks.caption: The attacker registers a user whose name ends in '--, then changes that user's password. Verified: afterwards ana's row holds 'pwned'.

blocks.md: Data is never trusted because of where it is stored. A value read from your own database, a file, a message queue or another service is still data, and it still needs a parameter when it goes into a query. OWASP's guidance (OWASP is the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a non-profit that publishes free security guidance) says the same controls apply whether a value comes from an HTTP request, another service or previously stored data.

**Defender view.** Each variant has a typical trace. UNION probing produces bursts of database errors about mismatched column counts. Boolean and time-based blind injection produce many near-identical requests to one endpoint that differ only in one parameter, often from one client, and time-based probes show up as slow queries and slow responses. Out-of-band injection shows up as unexpected DNS or outbound connections from the database server, which should normally make none. Second-order injection is the hardest: the bad query is triggered by an innocent-looking request, so code review that checks *every* query, not just those touching request data, matters most.

blocks.question: A search page shows no results and catches every database error, but it responds about five seconds slower for some inputs. What does this suggest?
options: Nothing: without visible output, SQL injection cannot be exploited
A UNION attack, since UNION queries are always slower
A cross-site scripting bug
Possible time-based blind injection: response time can leak whether an injected condition is true
blocks.explain: Blind injection needs only an observable difference. Time is observable. If an injected condition can make the query pause, the attacker learns one bit per request, and tools can repeat that thousands of times.

blocks.question: In the second-order example, sign-up used placeholders correctly. Why was the system still exploitable?
options: Placeholders do not work for INSERT statements
SQLite stored the name with the quote removed
A later query read the stored name back and pasted it into SQL text, trusting it because it came from the database
The attacker changed the sign-up code
blocks.explain: Placeholders protected the INSERT, so the name was stored exactly as typed, quote included. The bug is the UPDATE, which concatenates that stored value. Every query must bind its values, wherever they come from.

lessons.title: Heartland and TalkTalk: SQL injection as the way in

blocks.md:
Real breaches rarely end with the injection. SQL injection is usually the **initial access**, the first foothold, and the damage comes from what the attacker reaches next. Two cases show the pattern from both sides of the Atlantic.

**Heartland Payment Systems** was a New Jersey company that processed card payments for merchants; Heartland said it handled about 100 million transactions a month for some 250,000 businesses. In August 2009 US prosecutors indicted Albert Gonzalez, already awaiting trial over the earlier TJX retail breach, with two unnamed Russian conspirators for attacks on Heartland, the Hannaford supermarket chain, 7-Eleven and two national retailers.

According to the indictment as reported by Wired's Kim Zetter, the group picked targets from a list of Fortune 500 companies, studied their payment systems, and used **SQL injection** to get in: 7-Eleven in August 2007, Hannaford in November 2007 and Heartland on 26 December 2007. Once inside they installed **back doors** (hidden ways back in) and **sniffer** malware, programs that record network traffic passing a machine, here capturing card numbers in transit. They tested the malware against 20 antivirus products and programmed it to erase evidence.

The first Heartland foothold was in the corporate network, which was separate from the card-processing network. By May 2008 the attackers had moved into the processing network. Heartland learned of the breach only in January 2009, when card companies told it something was wrong.

blocks.title: Heartland: from SQL injection to discovery

scenes.caption: Month 0 is August 2007. SQL injection into 7-Eleven, then Hannaford in November 2007 (month 3), where 4.2 million card numbers were stolen.
26 December 2007 (about month 4.8): SQL injection into Heartland's corporate network. Back doors and sniffers follow.
By May 2008 (month 9) the attackers reach the separate card-processing network, where the sniffers capture card data in transit.
January 2009 (month 17): Heartland finds out after card companies raise the alarm. Indictment in August 2009 (month 24); Gonzalez is sentenced to 20 years in March 2010 (month 31).

blocks.md:
Prosecutors said the Heartland and Hannaford breaches together involved more than 130 million credit and debit card numbers, the largest US data-breach case prosecuted up to then. Heartland reported USD 12.6 million in costs by May 2009, including fines from Visa and MasterCard, which said it had not met the card industry's security rules; the company later put its losses at about USD 130 million, and Gonzalez was sentenced to 20 years in March 2010 ([Wired, 2010](https://www.wired.com/2010/03/heartland-sentencing/)).

**TalkTalk** is a UK broadband and phone provider. In October 2015 an attacker stole personal data of nearly 157,000 customers, including bank account details in nearly 16,000 cases. In October 2016 the ICO (Information Commissioner's Office, the UK data protection regulator) fined TalkTalk a then-record GBP 400,000.

The ICO's findings, as reported by the BBC: the attacker used **SQL injection** against three vulnerable web pages that came with Tiscali, a rival TalkTalk took over in 2009. The database software behind them was out of date, a fix for the bug existed, and TalkTalk did not know the pages were a problem, despite two earlier attacks in 2015 that should have warned it. Information Commissioner Elizabeth Denham said TalkTalk's "failure to implement the most basic cyber security measures allowed hackers to penetrate TalkTalk's systems with ease." TalkTalk said the attack cost it GBP 42 million and 101,000 subscribers left.

Both breaches started with a well-known bug class in a web page, and both turned into something much larger: lateral movement into a payment network in one case, and a forgotten set of acquired pages exposing a customer database in the other. You cannot fix pages you do not know you run, so asset inventory is a defence against injection too.

**Defender view.** What would have helped, mapped to this course:

- **Prevent**: parameterised queries everywhere (lesson 7), including in old and acquired code.
- **Limit**: a database account that can read only what each page needs, and network segmentation between corporate and processing networks (lesson 8). Heartland's segmentation slowed the attackers for months but did not stop them. Note also that an auditor had judged Heartland compliant with PCI DSS (the card industry's security standard) on 30 April 2008, shortly before the theft began: passing an audit is not the same as being secure.
- **Detect**: database error spikes and odd queries from web accounts (lesson 15). Heartland was told by outsiders; TalkTalk had earlier warning attacks.
- **Respond**: find every page built the same way, not just the one exploited.

blocks.question: In both the Heartland and TalkTalk cases, what role did SQL injection play?
options: It was used only after the attackers already had administrator access
It was the initial access: the first way into systems that the attackers then exploited further
It encrypted the victims' files for ransom
It was a false lead; the real cause was a stolen password
blocks.explain: In both cases SQL injection in a web-facing application gave the first foothold. At Heartland the attackers then installed back doors and sniffers and moved into the processing network; at TalkTalk the injection exposed customer data directly.

blocks.question: The ICO found that TalkTalk's vulnerable pages came from Tiscali, which it had acquired years earlier. Which control most directly addresses that root cause?
options: A longer password policy for staff
Encrypting backups
An inventory of every web application you expose, including acquired ones, with owners who patch and test them
Moving the database to a different vendor
blocks.explain: The pages were vulnerable, unpatched and apparently unknown to the people responsible. Knowing what you run, and giving each system an owner, is the precondition for fixing it.

blocks.md: The first idea most people have is to **escape** the input: rewrite each special character so the parser reads it as data. In standard SQL a quote inside a string literal is written twice, so the escaper doubles every quote. For the login example this works:

blocks.code:
def esc(s):
    return s.replace("'", "''")      # SQL-style quote doubling

pw = esc("' OR '1'='1")
query = f"SELECT id FROM users WHERE username = 'ana' AND password = '{pw}'"
# SELECT id FROM users WHERE username = 'ana' AND password = ''' OR ''1''=''1'
# returns no rows: the whole input is now one string literal
blocks.caption: Run with sqlite3. Every quote the attacker typed has become a doubled quote inside one literal, so the structure is unchanged.

blocks.title: Escaping doubles each quote so it stays inside the literal

scenes.caption: The attacker's input, grouped into pieces. Four of them are quote characters, each of which would end a string literal.
esc() doubles each quote. Inside a literal, two quotes mean one quote character, so the parser never finds the end of the string until the programmer's own closing quote.

blocks.md:
So why does OWASP call manual escaping "STRONGLY DISCOURAGED"? Because it only works if every one of these holds, everywhere, forever:

1. **The value is inside quotes.** Numbers usually are not, and there is nothing to escape.
2. **The value is a value.** Table and column names, and keywords like `ASC` and `DESC`, cannot be escaped into safety.
3. **The escaper matches the dialect.** Databases differ: MySQL also treats a backslash as an escape character inside strings unless its `NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES` mode is on, so an escaper written for one setting can be wrong for another.
4. **Nobody forgets.** One missed call site among hundreds of queries is enough.
5. **Escaped data is not reused raw.** Escaping changes the string for one query; read back from storage, it is raw again (the second-order bug).

blocks.title: Escaping a number field does nothing

scenes.output:
SELECT username FROM users WHERE id = 2
[('bob',)]
scenes.caption: Normal use: id 2 returns bob.

scenes.output:
SELECT username FROM users WHERE id = 2 OR 1=1
[('ana',), ('bob',), ('cy',)]
scenes.caption: The input has no quotes, so esc() changes nothing. The value is not inside a literal, so OR 1=1 is code. Every row comes back.

scenes.output: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '2 OR 1=1'
scenes.caption: Fixed: int() rejects anything that is not a whole number, and the placeholder means even a valid number never becomes SQL text.
The honest request still works.

blocks.md: Denylist filters ("block quotes, OR, UNION and --") are escaping's weaker cousin. They reject real input such as O'Brien, and they only stop the spellings someone thought of: SQL accepts comments, different case, different whitespace and many equivalent expressions. Lesson 9 shows a real product whose cleaning function was bypassed by finding a path where it was not applied.

Escaping still has a place, under its proper name: **output encoding**, transforming data for one specific output context with a library function written for that context. It is the main defence where no separate data channel exists: LDAP search filters (lesson 14), HTML pages (the client-side attacks course), and shell commands when a shell truly cannot be avoided. The rule is to use the library's encoder for that exact context, never a hand-written replace().

blocks.question: A developer escapes quotes in every input before building SQL. Which query is still injectable?
options: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '<escaped input>'
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = <escaped input>
Neither; escaping quotes fixes SQL injection
Both, because escaping never works
blocks.explain: In the numeric query the input is not inside quotes, so there is nothing for quote escaping to do, and input such as 5 OR 1=1 changes the logic. The string query is protected by correct escaping in this dialect, which is exactly the fragile kind of guarantee to avoid.

blocks.question: Why does OWASP prefer parameterised queries over correct escaping?
options: Escaping is slower
Parameterised queries encrypt the data
Escaping is not supported by modern databases
Escaping depends on context, dialect and configuration and must be done at every call site, while parameters keep values out of the SQL text entirely
blocks.explain: Correct escaping requires the right rules for the right context and database settings at every single call site. Parameters remove the problem: the SQL text is a constant and values never pass through the parser.

lessons.title: Parameterised queries: code and data on separate channels

blocks.md:
A **parameterised query** is SQL text with **placeholders** where values go: `?` in SQLite and many drivers, `$1, $2` in PostgreSQL, `:name` for named ones. The values are passed separately as **parameters** (also called bind variables). A **prepared statement** is the database-side object made from that text: the database parses and plans it once ("prepares" it), then can execute it many times with different values.

The security property comes from the order of events. The database finishes parsing the SQL text *before* the values exist. Each placeholder is already fixed as "one literal value goes here", so whatever the value contains, quotes and all, it can only ever be that value.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL's extended query protocol: text first, values later

scenes.caption: Parse: the driver sends only the SQL text with placeholders. The server parses it now. A Parse message may contain only one SQL statement.
Bind: the driver sends the values for $1 and $2. They are never parsed as SQL; they fill the slots the parser already created.
Execute: the server compares password with the literal text ' OR '1'='1. No user has that password, so zero rows come back.

blocks.md: You can watch this separation happen. With PostgreSQL's `log_statement` setting set to `all`, the server log records the statement text and its parameters on separate lines. This is the real log from running the login query through the extended protocol with the injection string as the password:

blocks.code:
LOG:  execute <unnamed>: SELECT id, username FROM users WHERE username = $1 AND password = $2
DETAIL:  Parameters: $1 = 'ana', $2 = ''' OR ''1''=''1'
blocks.caption: PostgreSQL 17, query sent with psql's `\bind` command (which uses Parse, Bind and Execute). The log quotes the parameter for display only; the server compared the raw text ' OR '1'='1 and returned 0 rows.

blocks.md: The same fix in four languages. PDO (PHP Data Objects) and JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) are the standard database interfaces of PHP and Java. In each, the SQL text is a constant and the values go in a separate argument:

blocks.caption: The vulnerable versions all share one feature: a + or an f-string inside the first argument.

blocks.md:
Some drivers **emulate** prepared statements: they fill the placeholders on the client side, quoting each value with the exact rules for that database, and send one string. PHP's PDO documents that it emulates prepared statements for drivers without native support. This is still safe for values, because the driver, not your code, does the quoting, and it does so for every value. What matters to you is the API shape: SQL text in one argument, values in another.

Placeholders have limits. They stand for **values only**: not table or column names, not keywords such as `ASC`/`DESC`, not a whole `IN (...)` list. PDO's manual says the same: if other parts of the query are built from unescaped input, injection is still possible.

blocks.code:
SORTS = {"name": "username", "newest": "id DESC"}    # fixed, app-owned choices

def list_users(sort):
    order = SORTS.get(sort, "username")      # unknown input falls back to a default
    return db.execute(f"SELECT username FROM users ORDER BY {order}").fetchall()

# list_users("newest")                 sorts by id DESC
# list_users("id; DROP TABLE users")   sorts by username: the input never reaches SQL

# A placeholder does NOT work here:
db.execute("SELECT username FROM users ORDER BY ?", ("id DESC",))
# runs, but sorts by the constant text 'id DESC', which is the same for every row
blocks.caption: Allowlist mapping for structure, as OWASP recommends. The f-string is safe only because order can hold just two strings the programmer wrote. Outputs verified in sqlite3.

blocks.md: Parameterise every value. Map every identifier and keyword through a fixed allowlist. Never quote a placeholder: in SQLite, `'?'` inside quotes is just a one-character string, and the call fails with "Incorrect number of bindings supplied"; Django's documentation warns against the same mistake with `'%s'`.

blocks.prompt: A colleague says: "Our queries are parameterised, so input validation is pointless." Are they right?
blocks.reveal: Partly. Parameters make validation unnecessary *for preventing SQL injection* in those values, and OWASP says validation complements binding and does not replace it. But validation still matters: it catches wrong types early (an id must be an integer), protects the parts placeholders cannot cover (sort columns), protects other interpreters the same value may reach later (a shell, a template), and keeps garbage out of your data.

blocks.question: A query is run as `execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", ("x' OR '1'='1",))`. What does the database do with the value?
options: Parses it as SQL, so every row is returned
Compares the name column with the literal text x' OR '1'='1 and returns rows with exactly that name
Rejects it because it contains quotes
Strips the quotes and searches for x OR 1=1
blocks.explain: The SQL text was parsed before the value arrived. The value fills a literal slot and is compared as plain text, quotes included. Usually no row matches.

blocks.question: A report page sorts by a column name taken from the URL. What is the right way to build that query?
options: Use a placeholder: ORDER BY ?
Escape quotes in the column name
Map the URL value to one of a fixed set of column names written in the code, and reject or default anything else
Put the column name inside quotes in the SQL
blocks.explain: Placeholders stand for values, so ORDER BY ? sorts by a constant. Quote escaping does nothing for an identifier. An allowlist means the SQL text only ever contains column names the programmer wrote.

lessons.title: ORMs, stored procedures and least-privilege accounts

blocks.md:
An **ORM** (object-relational mapper, or object-relational mapping) is a library that maps classes in your code to tables, and objects to rows, so you write `Person.objects.filter(username=name)` instead of SQL. Django's ORM, SQLAlchemy, Hibernate, ActiveRecord and Sequelize are examples. The ORM generates the SQL and binds values as parameters, so ordinary ORM calls are not injectable.

Every ORM also has **escape hatches** for the queries it cannot express: raw SQL methods, raw fragments inside ORM calls, or a direct database cursor. That is where injection comes back.

blocks.code:
# Django. Safe: the ORM binds name as a parameter
Person.objects.filter(username=name)

# VULNERABLE: raw() with an f-string
Person.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM app_person WHERE username = '{name}'")

# FIXED: raw() with params (Django uses %s placeholders on every backend)
Person.objects.raw("SELECT * FROM app_person WHERE username = %s", [name])

# Also wrong: quoting the placeholder yourself
Person.objects.raw("SELECT * FROM app_person WHERE username = '%s'", [name])
blocks.caption: Run against SQLite with Django: for name = x' OR '1'='1 the f-string version returned all three people and the params version returned none.

blocks.md:
ORMs with their own query language have their own injection. Hibernate, a Java ORM, uses HQL (Hibernate Query Language); OWASP's example builds `"from Inventory where productID='" + userSuppliedParameter + "'"`, which is injectable in exactly the SQL way, and the fix is the same: a named parameter, `productID=:productid`, set with `setParameter`.

A **stored procedure** is a named program stored inside the database (written in a procedural language such as PL/pgSQL, PostgreSQL's Procedural Language, or T-SQL, Transact-SQL, Microsoft's SQL dialect for SQL Server) that the application calls. Calling it with bound arguments is safe. But OWASP warns that binding the call does not protect **dynamic SQL inside the procedure**: if the procedure glues an argument into a SQL string and runs it with `EXECUTE` (PostgreSQL) or `EXEC` (SQL Server), the injection simply moves into the database.

blocks.code:
-- VULNERABLE: builds SQL text inside the procedure
CREATE FUNCTION find_bad(name text) RETURNS SETOF text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $f$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY EXECUTE
    'SELECT username FROM users WHERE username = ''' || name || '''';
END $f$;

-- FIXED: the argument is bound with USING, never pasted into the text
CREATE FUNCTION find_good(name text) RETURNS SETOF text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $f$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY EXECUTE 'SELECT username FROM users WHERE username = $1' USING name; END $f$;

SELECT * FROM find_bad('x'' OR ''1''=''1');    -- ana, bob, cy
SELECT * FROM find_good('x'' OR ''1''=''1');   -- (0 rows)
blocks.caption: Run on PostgreSQL 17 (verified). $f$ marks the start and end of the function body (PostgreSQL dollar quoting), RETURNS SETOF text means it returns rows of text, and || is SQL's string concatenation operator. Both are called the same safe way from the app; only the inside differs.

blocks.md:
**Least privilege** means every account gets only the permissions its job needs. It does not prevent injection; it limits what a successful injection can do, because injected SQL runs with the permissions of the application's database account.

OWASP's advice: never connect as a DBA (database administrator) or admin account; give each application, or each function, its own account; grant read-only access where reads are enough; rarely if ever grant create or delete rights; use **views** (saved queries that look like tables) to expose only the columns a page needs; and do not run the database server itself as root or SYSTEM. Recall the 1998 Phrack example, which connected as `sa`, the SQL Server system administrator: any injection there could do anything the database could.

blocks.code:
CREATE VIEW public_profiles AS SELECT id, username FROM users;   -- no password column
CREATE ROLE shop_app LOGIN;
GRANT SELECT ON public_profiles TO shop_app;                     -- and nothing else

SET ROLE shop_app;          -- act as the web app's account
SELECT * FROM public_profiles;   -- 3 rows: ana, bob, cy
SELECT password FROM users;      -- ERROR:  permission denied for table users
DROP TABLE users;                -- ERROR:  must be owner of table users
blocks.caption: Real PostgreSQL 17 output. Even if this app has an injection bug, its account cannot read passwords or drop tables.

blocks.title: What injected SQL can reach depends on the app's account

scenes.caption: The injection always runs as the application's database account. The question is what that account may touch.
Connected as an admin account (like sa in 1998): every table is readable and writable, and admin features may even reach the server's operating system.
Least privilege: SELECT on one view only. The same bug now leaks public usernames, which the page shows anyway, and every other request is refused with permission denied.

blocks.md: Permission-denied errors from the web application's own account are a high-value alert. A correctly written app never asks for tables it was not granted, so these errors usually mean a bug or an injection probing the edges.

blocks.question: A Java app calls a stored procedure with `prepareCall("{call find_user(?)}")` and `setString(1, input)`. Inside, the procedure builds a query with `'... WHERE name = ''' + @name + ''''` and runs it with EXEC. Is the app safe from SQL injection?
options: Yes, because the call uses a placeholder
Yes, because stored procedures cannot be injected
No: the input arrives safely as a value, but the procedure pastes it into new SQL text and runs it
No, because CallableStatement does not support parameters
blocks.explain: Binding protects the call, not the dynamic SQL constructed inside the procedure. The fix is inside the procedure: bind the value in the dynamic query (sp_executesql with parameters in SQL Server, EXECUTE ... USING in PostgreSQL) or avoid dynamic SQL.

blocks.question: What does least privilege on the database account achieve against SQL injection?
options: It prevents the injection from happening
It limits what injected SQL can read or change to what that account is allowed
It hides error messages from attackers
It makes UNION queries impossible
blocks.explain: The injected SQL runs as the app's account, so its permissions bound the damage. The injection itself still happens; least privilege is defence in depth, not a fix.

lessons.title: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims

blocks.md:
**MOVEit Transfer** is a managed file transfer (MFT) product from Progress Software: a web application that organisations run to exchange files securely with partners. It stores its data in MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server or Azure SQL.

According to CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and the FBI, from 27 May 2023 the Cl0p ransomware gang, also tracked as TA505, exploited a previously unknown SQL injection in MOVEit Transfer, CVE-2023-34362. CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is the public catalogue of named vulnerabilities. A flaw exploited before the vendor has a fix is called a **zero-day**: defenders had zero days of warning.

NIST's National Vulnerability Database describes the bug as a SQL injection in the MOVEit Transfer web application that let an **unauthenticated** attacker (no login needed) access the database, infer its structure and contents, and run SQL that alters or deletes data. Mandiant, Google's incident response firm, found the attackers used it to install a **web shell**: a small script placed on a web server that gives an attacker remote control through ordinary HTTP requests. This one, named LEMURLOOT, was written in C# and saved as `human2.aspx`, mimicking the product's real `human.aspx` page. It answered only requests carrying a secret password in a header, and could list and download stored files, read the Azure cloud storage settings, and create or delete users. Data was stolen sometimes within minutes.

blocks.title: The MOVEit attack chain, at advisory level

scenes.caption: Unauthenticated requests reach the web application. Mandiant saw POST requests to the legitimate guestaccess.aspx page before the web shell appeared, pointing at the injection there.
The injection gives the attacker the database: read, insert, change. Horizon3.ai's reconstruction shows inserted rows were then used to reach code execution.
A web shell named to blend in, human2.aspx, is installed. From here the attacker no longer needs the bug.
The shell lists and downloads files and reads storage settings. Cl0p stole data and demanded payment without encrypting anything.

blocks.md:
Why did the injection exist in a mature product? Horizon3.ai, a security company, compared the patched and unpatched code. One patched function, `UserGetUsersWithEmailAddress()`, changed from a **query concatenated from several arguments** to a SQL builder utility. The application did have a cleaning function, `XHTMLClean()`, that converted unsafe SQL characters to HTML-encoded forms, and Horizon3 could not get dangerous input through it on the direct path. Their working path instead used a header-parsing bug to reach an internal handler that set session variables from request headers, and those values reached queries **without passing through the cleaner**. Horizon3 noted their path may differ from the one Cl0p used.

That is lesson 6 in a real product: sanitising at the entrance fails when there is another entrance. Binding parameters at the query protects every path.

blocks.title: May to June 2023: exploitation, disclosure and response

scenes.caption: Day 0 is 27 May 2023, the earliest exploitation Mandiant found. Samples of the web shell were uploaded to VirusTotal (an online service that scans files with many antivirus engines) from 28 May.
Day 4, 31 May: Progress announces the vulnerability. Day 6, 2 June: the CVE is published in NVD and CISA adds it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue.
Day 6: Mandiant's analysis. Day 11, 7 June: CISA and FBI joint advisory with indicators and detection rules. Day 13, 9 June: Horizon3.ai's root-cause write-up.

blocks.md:
The scale came from the product, not the bug class: one injection in software that thousands of organisations exposed to the internet. Emsisoft, an antivirus company that tracked public disclosures, [counted](https://www.emsisoft.com/en/blog/44123/unpacking-the-moveit-breach-statistics-and-analysis/) 2,773 organisations and about 95.8 million individuals affected as of 28 June 2024, many of them through suppliers that used MOVEit on their behalf.

**Defender view**, from the advisories:

- Look in web server logs for POST requests to `guestaccess.aspx` followed by requests to unfamiliar `.aspx` files.
- Look for `human2.aspx` or `_human2.aspx` in the web root, and for user accounts named "Health Check Service", which the web shell created.
- Inspect database tables for unexpected inserted rows (Horizon3).
- CISA's advisory includes YARA rules (YARA is a pattern-matching tool for finding malware files) for LEMURLOOT.
- Respond by patching, then assume compromise: hunt for web shells and new accounts, since patching does not remove them.

Patching closes the door but does not evict anyone already inside. After an injection that may have been exploited, look for persistence (web shells, new accounts, changed configuration) and for what data left, using web, database and network logs.

blocks.question: MOVEit had a function that converted unsafe SQL characters before input reached queries. Why did that not prevent CVE-2023-34362, according to Horizon3.ai's analysis?
options: Attackers found a path where values reached SQL without passing through the cleaning function
The function had a typo in its character list
The database ignored HTML encoding
Cleaning functions only work on MySQL
blocks.explain: Their reconstruction reached the injection through session variables set from request headers, which bypassed XHTMLClean(). Cleaning at the input relies on every path being cleaned; a parameterised query is safe whichever path the value took.

blocks.question: You patched MOVEit on 3 June 2023. What should you do next?
options: Nothing: the patch removes the vulnerability and any damage
Rotate the TLS certificate
Hunt for signs of earlier compromise, such as human2.aspx files, "Health Check Service" accounts and unusual requests in web logs
Switch the database engine
blocks.explain: Exploitation began on 27 May, before any patch existed. A web shell installed before patching keeps working afterwards, so you must look for persistence and data theft, then remove and report them.

lessons.title: NoSQL injection: when a value turns into an operator

blocks.md:
**NoSQL** is a loose name for databases that do not use SQL tables; it is read as "not only SQL" or "non-relational". **MongoDB**, the most widely used, stores **documents**: JSON-like records with named fields (JSON is JavaScript Object Notation, the `{"key": "value"}` text format). Internally they are stored as BSON (Binary JSON). A collection of documents plays the role of a table.

A MongoDB query is not a string; it is an object describing what to match. `{username: "ana"}` matches documents whose username is ana. Conditions other than equality use **operators**, keys that start with `$`: `$ne` (not equal), `$gt` (greater than), `$in` (in a list), `$regex` (matches a pattern), and `$where`, which runs a JavaScript expression on the server.

MongoDB's own FAQ points out that because a client builds a query as a BSON object, not a string, "traditional SQL injection attacks are not a problem": a quote or brace in a value is just a character. But OWASP's NoSQL guidance adds the catch: building a query object does not prevent **operator injection** when an untrusted value is itself an object. If a field the code expected to be a string arrives as `{"$ne": ""}`, MongoDB reads it as an operator, not a value.

blocks.caption: The textbook illustration from PortSwigger. Express is a Node.js web framework; express.json() turns a JSON body into a JavaScript object. Toy code compares plain passwords; real code compares a password hash, which also blocks this specific trick, but the same bug works on any filter field.

blocks.title: The query object the database receives

scenes.caption: Honest login. Both fields hold strings, and MongoDB matches them by equality: ana's document only if the password equals rose.
Attack body. JSON parsing turned the password field into an object whose key is the operator $ne. MongoDB reads it as the condition password is not equal to the empty string.
Every real password is non-empty, so ana's document matches and the attacker is logged in. No quote characters were needed: the type changed, not the text.

blocks.md: Forms can do this too. PortSwigger notes that URL-encoded inputs can carry operators as `username[$ne]=invalid` when the server's parser turns bracketed names into nested objects.

The fixes, from OWASP and PortSwigger:

- **Check types before building the query.** If a field must be a string, reject anything else. This is the core fix.
- **Validate the whole body against a schema** (required fields, types, lengths) with a validation library, or use an ODM (object-document mapper, MongoDB's version of an ORM) whose schema casts values.
- **Never pass client-supplied objects through as filters**, and allowlist which fields and operators a search may use.
- **Avoid `$where`**, `mapReduce`, `$function` and `$accumulator` with user input: they run JavaScript on the server. If you do not use them, MongoDB documents turning server-side JavaScript off with `--noscripting` or `security.javascriptEnabled: false`.

blocks.caption: The type check is the injection fix. Looking the user up by name and verifying a password hash in code is the authentication fix; verifyPassword stands for a library call such as bcrypt or argon2.

blocks.prompt: A teammate proposes rejecting any request body whose JSON text contains the characters `"$`. Does that solve operator injection?
blocks.reveal: It blocks the common case but OWASP calls it a denylist, not an allowlist: it also rejects legitimate strings that start with $ (a price, a password), and it says nothing about which fields and types are allowed. Field-by-field type and schema validation is the real fix, with the string check at most an extra layer.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Operator injection leaves different traces from SQL injection: there are no syntax errors. Look for request bodies or query strings whose keys start with `$` or contain brackets, for spikes in 400 responses once validation is in place, and for logins that succeed with no matching password-failure history. MongoDB's own profiler and logs show query shapes; a filter with `$ne` on a password field from the login endpoint should never occur.

blocks.question: Why does a JSON body `{"password": {"$ne": ""}}` bypass a MongoDB login that uses `findOne({username, password})`?
options: MongoDB parses the password string as SQL
The value is an object, so MongoDB treats $ne as an operator and matches any non-empty password
The $ character disables authentication
MongoDB ignores fields it does not recognise
blocks.explain: No string was parsed. JSON allowed the client to send an object where the code expected a string, and objects with $ keys are operators in MongoDB queries.

blocks.question: Which single change most directly prevents operator injection in that login handler?
options: Escaping quotes in the password
Using HTTPS
Rejecting the request unless username and password are both plain strings
Renaming the password field
blocks.explain: The attack changes the value's type, not its characters, so escaping does nothing. A strict type check (or schema validation) ensures only plain strings reach the query.

lessons.title: OS command injection: the shell is an interpreter too

blocks.md:
A **shell** is the program that reads command lines and starts other programs. On Linux and macOS the standard one is `sh`, and **bash** (the Bourne-Again SHell of the GNU Project, the free-software project that rewrote the standard Unix tools; named after the earlier Bourne shell it replaced) is the most common. When a program runs `sh -c "some text"`, the shell parses that text:

- Spaces split it into **words**; the first word is the program, the rest its **arguments** (the list `argv` the program receives).
- `;`, `&&`, `||`, `&`, `|` and newline separate or chain **commands**.
- `$(...)` and backticks run a command and paste its output in (**command substitution**).
- `>` and `<` redirect output and input to files; quotes group words.

These are **shell metacharacters**. PortSwigger lists `&`, `&&`, `|` and `||` as separators on both Windows and Unix, and `;` and newline on Unix.

**OS command injection** happens when a program builds a shell command line from input. A typical case is a web page that runs a system tool, such as looking up a host name. In Python, `os.system()` and `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)` hand one string to `/bin/sh -c`; in Node, `child_process.exec()` does the same. To keep the demo harmless, the "tool" here is `echo`, which just prints its arguments:

blocks.caption: Real outputs (Python 3, Node 22). INJECTED is printed by a second command the attacker added; in a real attack it would be any command the web server's user may run.

blocks.title: How /bin/sh splits the command line

scenes.caption: Simplified (ex.com stands for example.com, look for looking, INJ for INJECTED). The shell splits on spaces and finds the separator ;, so it runs two commands.

With an argument list there is no shell. The program receives argv directly: three entries, echo, looking up (one argument, shown as lk up) and the whole input as one argument. The ; is just a character in it.

blocks.code:
# FIXED (Python): pass a list; no shell is involved
subprocess.run(["echo", "looking up", host], capture_output=True, text=True)
# host = "example.com; echo INJECTED" prints: looking up example.com; echo INJECTED

// FIXED (Node.js): execFile runs the program directly, without a shell
execFile("echo", ["looking up", host], cb);

# If a shell is unavoidable on Linux or macOS, quote each value for the shell:
import shlex
subprocess.run(f"echo looking up {shlex.quote(host)}", shell=True)
blocks.caption: Python's subprocess documentation: it does not implicitly call a shell, so all characters, metacharacters included, can safely be passed to child processes; with shell=True quoting becomes the application's job. Node's docs: execFile does not spawn a shell by default.

blocks.md:
An argument list removes the shell, but the target program still parses its own arguments. **Argument injection** is when input becomes an *option*: a host name that starts with `-` may be read as a flag. OWASP's example is escaped input passed to curl that is simply `--help`; with options that read or write files the impact can be far worse. Defences, from OWASP's command injection cheat sheet:

1. **Avoid running commands at all.** Use a library call instead: Python's `socket.getaddrinfo()` resolves a host name without starting any program.
2. **Validate with an allowlist**: for a host name, letters, digits, dots and hyphens only, not starting with `-`.
3. **End option parsing** with `--` where the program supports it, so later words are never options.
4. **Run with least privilege**, so an injected command can do little.

One more trap from Python's documentation: on Windows, `.bat` and `.cmd` files may be run through a shell even without shell=True.

blocks.title: Validating a host name before using it

scenes.caption: Only allowed characters and no leading hyphen: accepted.

scenes.output:
example.com True
example.com; echo x False
scenes.caption: The ; and space are not in the allowlist, so fullmatch fails. An allowlist says what is allowed, so it does not need to know every metacharacter.

scenes.output:
example.com True
example.com; echo x False
-oProxyCommand=x False
scenes.caption: The = is not allowed and the leading hyphen check would reject it anyway: no input can become an option.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Command injection leaves a trail in process creation logs: a web server's worker process (for example `www-data` running a Python or PHP app, or `w3wp.exe`, the worker process of IIS, Internet Information Services, Microsoft's web server) starting `sh -c` or `cmd.exe /c` with separators in the command line, or starting tools a web app never uses. Linux audit logging and Windows process creation auditing record these. In code review, search for `shell=True`, `os.system`, `os.popen`, `exec(` and backtick strings, and in PHP for `system`, `exec`, `shell_exec` and `passthru`.

blocks.question: Which Python call is safe against shell injection when `name` is untrusted?
options: subprocess.run(f"grep {name} log.txt", shell=True)
os.system("grep " + name + " log.txt")
subprocess.run(["grep", "--", name, "log.txt"])
subprocess.run("grep " + name.replace(";", "") + " log.txt", shell=True)
blocks.explain: The list form starts grep directly with name as one argument, so shell metacharacters mean nothing, and -- stops grep from reading name as an option. Removing ; leaves &&, |, $( ) and newlines.

blocks.question: A Node app switched from `exec()` to `execFile("tar", ["-czf", out, input])`. A user submits `input = "--checkpoint-action=..."`. What risk remains?
options: None: execFile makes all input safe
Argument injection: tar may read the value as an option rather than a file name
SQL injection
Shell metacharacter injection through ;
blocks.explain: There is no shell, so metacharacters are inert, but tar still parses its own argv. A value starting with - can be treated as an option. Validate names, put -- before file arguments where supported, or avoid the command.

lessons.title: Shellshock: when an environment variable became code

blocks.md:
Every process carries **environment variables**: name=value strings such as `HOME=/home/ana` that it passes on to programs it starts. They are meant to be plain data.

In the early web, the standard way for a server to run a program per request was **CGI** (Common Gateway Interface, a "gateway" between the web server and other programs, specified in RFC 3875). The server passes request details to the program as environment variables. RFC 3875 says each HTTP request header becomes a variable named `HTTP_` plus the header name in capitals with `-` turned into `_`. So the `User-Agent` header, which the client can set to any text, arrives as `HTTP_USER_AGENT`.

Bash had a feature for passing **functions** (named blocks of shell code) to child bash processes: it exported them as environment variables whose value started with `() {`. When bash started, it scanned its environment and imported any variable that looked like a function by parsing the value as a function definition.

The bug: after parsing the function body, bash **kept going and executed whatever followed** the closing brace. The researcher Stephane Chazelas found it, and Florian Weimer announced it on 24 September 2014 on oss-security, a public list where open-source developers and vendors discuss security flaws, as CVE-2014-6271, soon nicknamed **Shellshock**. NVD's description: GNU Bash through 4.3 processes trailing strings after function definitions in the values of environment variables. It was remotely reachable through the CGI modules of the Apache HTTP Server (an open-source web server), OpenSSH (the common remote-login server) accounts locked to one command by ForceCommand, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, which hands out network settings) clients and more.

blocks.title: How a vulnerable bash read one environment variable

scenes.caption: A variable value from the published test of Red Hat, a Linux vendor. To bash at startup, a value beginning with () { looks like an exported function. (vuln stands for the word vulnerable.)
Bash parses the function: its body is : (the do-nothing command) and it ends at the closing brace. This much is the intended feature.
The bug: a vulnerable bash then executed the rest of the string, here echo vulnerable, as a command, immediately at startup, before running the script it was asked to run.

Patched bash stops at the end of the function and refuses trailing code. The final fix went further and only imports functions from specially prefixed variable names, so an ordinary header-derived variable is never parsed as code.

blocks.code:
$ env x='() { :;}; echo vulnerable' bash -c "echo this is a test"
vulnerable          (printed only by an unpatched bash)
this is a test

# On a patched bash "this is a test" is printed; bashes with only the first
# patch also print "warning: x: ignoring function definition attempt".
# (Output above from Red Hat's advisory. Run on macOS's patched bash 3.2.57,
#  only "this is a test" appeared.)
blocks.caption: Red Hat's one-line local check: run it only on your own machine. env sets x for one command; bash -c runs a harmless script. The test never touches a network.

blocks.title: Shellshock through a CGI script

scenes.caption: The client sends a request whose User-Agent header contains a function-like value. Headers are entirely client-controlled.
Following RFC 3875, the server copies the header into the environment as HTTP_USER_AGENT and starts the script, which is written in bash.
At startup the vulnerable bash imports the function and runs the trailing command, with the web server's privileges, before the script's own first line.

blocks.md:
Red Hat's advisory explains why so many systems were exposed: bash runs behind the scenes far more than people realise. A CGI script did not have to be *written* in bash; it was enough to start a shell where /bin/sh is bash (Red Hat, macOS; Debian and Ubuntu use dash, which was not affected), and `system()` and `popen()` in C, `os.system()` and `os.popen()` in Python, and `system()` and `exec()` in PHP running as CGI all do. DHCP clients run shell scripts with values from the network's DHCP server, usually as root.

The first patch was incomplete (the follow-up became CVE-2014-7169), and Michal Zalewski (a security researcher who blogs as lcamtuf) and others found more parser bugs by fuzzing, feeding the parser huge numbers of automatically varied inputs. By 30 September, six days after disclosure, Cloudflare, whose network sits in front of many websites, [reported](https://blog.cloudflare.com/inside-shellshock/) blocking over 1.1 million Shellshock attempts, mostly reconnaissance and attempts to take control of servers, plus some denial of service.

Shellshock is injection into an interpreter nobody thought was in the path. The data (a header) was never concatenated into code by the application; the interpreter itself treated a data channel (the environment) as code. Know which interpreters your input reaches, including the ones your libraries start for you.

**Defender view.** Prevent: patch bash (Linux vendors and Apple shipped fixes); remove CGI scripts and shell calls from web paths; do not copy untrusted data into the environment of a shell. Detect: the string `() {` at the start of a header value has no legitimate use, so web access logs that record User-Agent and Referer, and WAF (web application firewall) rules, caught attempts easily; Cloudflare's analysis was built from its WAF logs. Respond: on any host that ran an unpatched bash behind CGI, assume commands were run as the web server user and check for planted files and outbound connections.

blocks.question: A Python CGI script, not a bash script, runs `os.system("/usr/bin/uptime")` with no user input in the command. Was it exposed to Shellshock on a server with vulnerable bash as /bin/sh?
options: No: the command contains no user input
Yes: os.system starts a shell, which inherits the HTTP_ variables from CGI and parses them at startup
No: Python scripts are immune
Only if the script was run as root
blocks.explain: The attacker's data is in the environment, not the command line. os.system runs /bin/sh -c, and a vulnerable bash as /bin/sh imports function-like variables at startup and runs the trailing code.

blocks.question: What did the final fix for Shellshock change?
options: Bash only imports functions from variables with special prefixed names and stops at the end of the function body
It removed environment variables from Linux
Web servers stopped passing headers to CGI
It disabled bash functions entirely
blocks.explain: After the first patch was found incomplete, bash moved exported functions to specially named variables, so arbitrary variables such as HTTP_USER_AGENT are never parsed as function definitions.

blocks.md:
A **template** is text with holes in it: a page or email with placeholders that a **template engine** fills in with data at run time. Jinja2 (Python; Jinja is Japanese for a Shinto shrine, or temple, chosen because temple sounds like template), Twig (PHP), FreeMarker (Java) and Handlebars (JavaScript) are template engines. In Jinja2, `{{ name }}` prints a variable and `{% for u in users %}` runs a loop. Template syntax is a small programming language: expressions inside `{{ }}` are **evaluated**, on the server, before the page is sent.

So a template engine is an interpreter, and **server-side template injection** (SSTI) is the bug where user input becomes part of the *template source* instead of being passed in as data. James Kettle, director of research at PortSwigger, first documented the technique in 2015 and presented it at Black Hat USA, a security conference.

blocks.caption: Real outputs with Jinja2 3.1. Note that autoescape is on and the bug is still there.

blocks.title: Template source versus template data

scenes.caption: Honest input. The template source happens to contain no template syntax, so it renders as itself.
The input contains template syntax. It is now part of the source, so the engine parses {{ 7*7 }} as an expression and evaluates it on the server. 49 is PortSwigger's classic detection probe.
Fixed. The source is a constant the programmer wrote, parsed before any input arrives. name is data: the engine prints its characters and never parses them.

blocks.md:
Why it is serious: template expressions can usually reach the objects passed to the template and, through them, the language runtime. Kettle's research showed remote code execution in several popular engines, including escapes from **sandboxes** (restricted modes meant to make untrusted templates safe). PortSwigger notes that engines differ in detail: `{{7*'7'}}` gives 49 in Twig but 7777777 in Jinja2, which is how testers tell engines apart.

SSTI often appears where users are *meant* to customise text: marketing emails, wiki pages, notification templates. Kettle's first example was a bulk email tool that let users edit the greeting template.

Auto-escaping does not stop SSTI. It encodes HTML special characters in the *output* to prevent cross-site scripting, but injected template syntax is evaluated before any output exists. OWASP's SSTI cheat sheet says this explicitly, and the demo above shows 49 with autoescape on.

Defences, from OWASP and PortSwigger, in order:

1. **Never build template source from user input.** Templates are code; user values go in as variables, as in `greet_fixed`.
2. **If users must write templates**, use a **logic-less** engine such as Mustache (no expressions, only substitution), or the engine's sandbox: Jinja2's `SandboxedEnvironment`, Twig's sandbox with a strict security policy. Treat sandboxes as a layer, not a guarantee; they have been escaped.
3. **Keep the render context minimal**: pass only the values a template needs, never secrets, configuration or service objects.
4. **Isolate** template rendering of untrusted templates, for example in a locked-down container, as PortSwigger suggests.

**Defender view**: template syntax such as `{{`, `${` or `<%` in form fields and query strings, WAF rules for template probes (OWASP's Core Rule Set added template injection detection), and template engine exceptions in application logs.

**Pointer: Equifax 2017.** A related class is injection into a framework's own **expression language**. In March 2017 Apache Struts 2, a Java web framework, fixed a bug (advisory S2-045, CVE-2017-5638) in its Jakarta multipart parser: a malformed `Content-Type` header caused an exception whose error-message handling let the header's content run commands on the server. Attackers began exploiting it within days. Equifax (recall the security-basics lesson on its missed patch) was alerted on 8 March but did not patch one system; according to the US House Oversight Committee, attackers entered it on 13 May 2017, stayed 76 days, and the breach affected 148 million people. The server-side attacks course covers it in depth.

blocks.question: A support tool lets agents type a custom reply that is rendered with `Template(agent_text).render(customer=c)`. A customer cannot edit agent_text. Is there an SSTI risk, and from whom?
options: No risk: only templates in files can be injected
Yes: anyone who can write agent_text, such as an agent or a compromised agent account, can run template expressions on the server
Yes: any customer can inject through their name
No: autoescape prevents it
blocks.explain: agent_text is template source, so whoever controls it controls code on the server. Customers' names arrive as data (c) and are safe. If agents must write templates, use a logic-less engine or a sandbox with a minimal context.

blocks.question:
Which change fixes `render_template_string("

" + request.args["title"] + "

")` in a Flask (Python web framework) app?
options: Turn on autoescape
Strip the characters { and } from title

Use a constant template and pass title as a variable: render_template_string("

{{ title }}

", title=request.args["title"])
Use HTTPS
blocks.explain: The fix moves the input from template source to template data. Autoescape only affects output encoding, and stripping braces is a denylist that may miss other syntax such as {% %} or engine-specific forms.

lessons.title: LDAP, XPath, header and log injection

blocks.md:
The same mistake appears wherever a program builds text for a parser. Four more parsers, briefly.

**LDAP** (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is how programs query **directories**: central databases of users, groups and devices, such as Microsoft Active Directory. It is "lightweight" because it was designed to reach X.500 directories (an older international directory standard) without the resource requirements of X.500's own Directory Access Protocol (DAP). Programs often use it to check logins. An LDAP **search filter** is written in prefix notation, the operator before its operands: `(&(uid=ana)(objectClass=person))` means uid is ana AND objectClass is person; `*` is a wildcard that matches anything.

blocks.code:
# VULNERABLE: input pasted into the filter
f"(&(uid={user})(objectClass=person))"
#   user = "*"             gives (&(uid=*)(objectClass=person))          every person
#   user = "ana)(uid=*"    gives (&(uid=ana)(uid=*)(objectClass=person)) a new clause

# FIXED: RFC 4515 escaping of * ( ) \ and NUL as backslash + two hex digits
def ldap_filter_escape(value):
    return "".join("\\%02x" % ord(c) if c in "*()\\\x00" else c for c in value)

f"(&(uid={ldap_filter_escape(user)})(objectClass=person))"
#   user = "*"            gives (&(uid=\2a)(objectClass=person))   a literal asterisk
#   user = "ana)(uid=*"   gives (&(uid=ana\29\28uid=\2a)(objectClass=person))
blocks.caption: Run in Python 3. Prefer your LDAP library's encoder over this sketch; OWASP notes that distinguished names (RFC 4514) use different escaping rules from search filters (RFC 4515).

blocks.title: An LDAP filter before and after escaping

scenes.caption: Input ana)(uid=* unescaped. Its ) closes the uid clause and its ( opens a new one, (uid=*), which every entry matches. (obj.. stands for objectClass=person.)
Escaped per RFC 4515: ) becomes `\29`, ( becomes `\28` and * becomes `\2a`. They are now part of the value, so the filter keeps its two intended clauses and simply finds no such uid.

blocks.md:
